name: MathlibAnnex.ContinuousLinearMap.abs_det_sub_le_max
title: A determinant difference bound in the sup operator norm

content.display_title: A determinant difference bound in the sup operator norm
content.one_sentence_role: Controls determinant variation by replacing one matrix row at a time.
content.natural_language_statement:
Let $I$ be a finite set of size $n$, and give $\mathbb R^I$ the sup norm $\|x\|_\infty=\max_{i\in I}|x_i|$ (the zero norm on the zero space if $I=\varnothing$). For continuous real-linear maps $P,Q:\mathbb R^I\to\mathbb R^I$, use the induced operator norm. If $n\ge1$, then

$$|\det P-\det Q|\le
n\max\{\|P\|,\|Q\|\}^{\,n-1}\|P-Q\|.$$

For $n=0$, both determinants are $1$ and the bound is $0\le0$.
content.assumptions: The coordinate set $I$ is finite and may be empty. The coefficients are real and the operator norm is induced by the sup norm on both domain and codomain. Neither map is assumed invertible.
content.conclusion: The coefficient $n$ counts the number of row replacements. The norm is specifically the sup operator norm; the estimate is not being asserted here with an unspecified norm on the same coordinate space.
content.proof_summary: The determinant is bounded by the product of the absolute row sums. A sign vector bounds each such row sum by the sup operator norm. In a one-row replacement, one row is a row of $P-Q$ and the other $n-1$ rows are rows of $P$ or $Q$; summing the $n$ replacement bounds gives the result.

proof_steps.text:
**Bound a determinant by its row sums.** Let $C=(C_{ij})_{i,j\in I}$ be a real square matrix, and let $\mathfrak S(I)$ denote the permutations of $I$. Expanding the determinant gives

$$\begin{aligned}
|\det C|
&=\left|\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak S(I)}
\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i\in I}C_{i,\sigma(i)}\right|\\
&\le\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak S(I)}\prod_{i\in I}|C_{i,\sigma(i)}|\\
&\le\sum_{f:I\to I}\prod_{i\in I}|C_{i,f(i)}|\\
&=\prod_{i\in I}\left(\sum_{j\in I}|C_{ij}|\right).
\end{aligned}$$

The second inequality includes all functions $f:I\to I$, rather than only bijections; every added summand is nonnegative. The last equality is distributivity: expanding the product chooses one column $f(i)$ independently in each row. This is precisely the row-sum bound needed below, not a bound by Euclidean row lengths.

**Bound each row sum by the operator norm.** Let $C$ now be the standard matrix of a continuous real-linear map $T:\mathbb R^I\to\mathbb R^I$, so $C_{ij}=(Te_j)_i$ for the coordinate vector $e_j$. For a fixed row $i$, choose

$$\varepsilon^{(i)}_j=
\begin{cases}1,&C_{ij}\ge0,\\-1,&C_{ij}<0.\end{cases}
\qquad \|\varepsilon^{(i)}\|_\infty\le1.$$

Then $C_{ij}\varepsilon^{(i)}_j=|C_{ij}|$, and therefore

$$\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j\in I}|C_{ij}|
&=\left|(T\varepsilon^{(i)})_i\right|\\
&\le\|T\varepsilon^{(i)}\|_\infty
\le\|T\|\,\|\varepsilon^{(i)}\|_\infty
\le\|T\|.
\end{aligned}$$

Apply this with $T=P$, $T=Q$, and $T=P-Q$. These three applications provide the bounds for every row appearing in the next step.

**Estimate one row replacement.** Assume $n\ge1$ and choose one enumeration of $I$ for both rows and columns. Write $P_{ij}=(Pe_j)_i$ and $Q_{ij}=(Qe_j)_i$. Define

$$(C_k)_{ij}=\begin{cases}P_{ij},&i\le k,\\Q_{ij},&i>k,\end{cases}
\qquad 0\le k\le n.$$

Thus $C_0$ is the matrix of $Q$ and $C_n$ that of $P$. For $1\le k\le n$, let $D_k$ have row $k$ equal to $(P-Q)_{k,\bullet}$ and every other row equal to that of $C_{k-1}$. Linearity of the determinant in row $k$ gives

$$\det C_k-\det C_{k-1}=\det D_k.$$

Step 2 bounds the row sums of $D_k$ by

$$\sum_j|(D_k)_{ij}|\le
\begin{cases}\|P-Q\|,&i=k,\\
\max\{\|P\|,\|Q\|\},&i\ne k.
\end{cases}$$

Substituting these bounds into Step 1 yields

$$|\det C_k-\det C_{k-1}|
\le\max\{\|P\|,\|Q\|\}^{\,n-1}\|P-Q\|.$$

There is one difference row and exactly $n-1$ other rows. For $n=1$, the product over the other rows is the empty product $1$.

**Sum the $n$ replacement bounds.** Since $C_0=Q$ and $C_n=P$ in the standard coordinates,

$$\begin{aligned}
|\det P-\det Q|
&=\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n}(\det C_k-\det C_{k-1})\right|\\
&\le\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\det C_k-\det C_{k-1}|\\
&\le n\max\{\|P\|,\|Q\|\}^{\,n-1}\|P-Q\|.
\end{aligned}$$

This is the stated bound. If $n=0$, there are no replacements and both empty determinants are $1$, giving $0\le0$ separately.

content.lean_realization_notes: The row estimate uses the sum of the absolute values of entries, not the Euclidean length of a row. This fits the sup norm through a sign vector. All coordinate matrices refer to the standard coordinate basis, so their determinants are the determinants of the original linear maps.
